title: "A regimen approved without a trial"
subtitle: "Lesson C-02"
description: >
  Pembrolizumab's every-six-weeks regimen entered the label with no new efficacy
  study. The argument was exposure matching, and it is worth understanding both
  because it worked and because it is easy to misuse.
categories: [regulatory, exposure-response, biologics, approved drugs]

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## The decision this serves
Your antibody is approved every three weeks. Clinicians want every six — fewer
infusion visits, less travel, less chair time. A new phase 3 would take years,
cost a fortune, and randomise patients to a question that is about convenience
rather than survival.

Can you change the regimen on modelling alone? Sometimes. This lesson is about
when, and about the four conditions that have to hold first.
:::

## 1. What was actually approved

Pembrolizumab was approved in 2014 at 2 mg/kg every three weeks
([BLA 125514](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/cder/daf/index.cfm?event=overview.process&ApplNo=125514)),
later 200 mg flat Q3W. In 2020 a **400 mg every six weeks** regimen was added
to the label. No new efficacy trial was run for it.

The supporting analysis is Lala et al.
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejca.2020.02.016)): a population PK model built
on **2,993 subjects across five trials**, used to simulate the new regimen and
compare its exposure with the approved one.

That is the whole argument. A model, an exposure comparison, and a label change.

## 2. What exposure matching claims

The claim is a syllogism, and it is worth writing out because each line can fail
independently:

1. Clinical effect is driven by **exposure**, not by dose.
2. The relationship between exposure and effect is **known** over some range.
3. The new regimen produces exposure **inside that range**, matching the
   approved regimen on the metric that drives effect.
4. Therefore the new regimen produces the same effect.

Nothing here is about pharmacology being kind. It is about having already
purchased the expensive information — the exposure–response relationship — and
reusing it rather than buying it twice.

## 3. Three metrics, three jobs

"Matching exposure" is meaningless until you say *which* exposure. Three
summaries of the same concentration–time curve do different work.

| Metric | What it is | What it argues |
|---|---|---|
| **C~avg~** | average concentration over the interval | efficacy: total drug delivered |
| **C~min~** | trough, just before the next dose | target coverage: does receptor occupancy lapse? |
| **C~max~** | peak, just after dosing | safety: is this a concentration anyone has tolerated? |

Doubling the dose and doubling the interval holds **C~avg~ constant by
construction** — same amount of drug per unit time. That part is arithmetic, not
pharmacology, and on its own it proves nothing. The work is in the other two.

Q6W necessarily has a **higher peak** and a **lower trough** than Q3W. Both have
to be defended, and they are defended differently.

## 4. The bracketing argument

Here is the move that makes this legitimate rather than hopeful.

For the trough, Lala et al. report that fewer than 1% of subjects had a
transiently lower C~min~ than under the approved regimens — and that even with
those reductions, similar target saturation is expected. The claim is not that
the trough is identical. It is that the trough stays above the concentration
where occupancy would fall off.

For the peak, the projected C~max~ for 400 mg Q6W was roughly **65% lower** than
that of 10 mg/kg Q2W — a regimen already given to patients as the maximum
clinical dose. The new peak is not merely acceptable in the abstract; it is
**below a peak that has already been tolerated in trials**.

That is the shape of the argument. The exposure–response relationship had been
characterised over a **five-fold dose range**, from 2 mg/kg Q3W up to 10 mg/kg
Q2W. The new regimen sits *inside* that. Nobody is extrapolating beyond the
data; they are interpolating within it.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## The distinction that carries the whole lesson
**Interpolation inside a studied exposure range is a modelling claim.
Extrapolation beyond it is a hypothesis.** Regulators treat these very
differently, and so should you. The five-fold dose range in the pembrolizumab
programme was not a lucky accident — the wide dose-ranging done early is
precisely what made the later regimen change cheap.
:::

## 5. The four conditions

Exposure matching is admissible when all four hold. Check them explicitly.

1. **The exposure metric is the right one.** Efficacy is driven by C~avg~ for
   this class; for a time-above-threshold antibiotic it would not be.
2. **A population PK model exists that is credible for extrapolation** — built
   on enough subjects, with covariates characterised, and validated.
3. **The exposure–response relationship is established over a range that
   brackets the new regimen** on every metric that matters.
4. **The E–R relationship is flat, or at least shallow, across that range.** If
   effect changes steeply with exposure, a small mismatch matters and matching
   "closely enough" stops being good enough.

Fail any one and this becomes a hypothesis requiring a trial.

## 6. Read the correction too

The 2020 paper carries a corrigendum
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejca.2020.12.006)). It is short, and this
curriculum cites it alongside the paper deliberately: a lesson about reading
regulatory arguments carefully has no business quoting a source without its
published correction.

## Work through it

The notebook reproduces the argument. A two-compartment model, both regimens
simulated to steady state, and the three metrics computed and compared — the
C~avg~ match, the trough dip, and the peak checked against the highest dose ever
given.

## Failure mode — matching the wrong metric on a steep curve

Two ways this goes wrong, and neither errors.

**A steep exposure–response.** Suppose effect rises sharply with C~min~ rather
than plateauing. Now a trough 20% lower is not a rounding difference — it is a
different drug. The C~avg~ match still looks perfect, because C~avg~ was held
constant by arithmetic. Your table of exposure metrics will show a beautiful
result for a regimen that loses efficacy.

**Matching outside the studied range.** Push to Q12W. C~avg~ still matches
exactly — it is arithmetic. But the peak now exceeds anything given to a patient,
and the trough falls below anything observed. Every number in the comparison
table is computable, and none of them is supported.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## The habit
Before presenting an exposure-matching argument, plot the **exposure–response
curve with the new regimen's exposures marked on it**. If the markers fall
outside the range of the data the curve was fitted to, you do not have an
argument; you have an extrapolation wearing one.
:::

## Check yourself

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. Doubling dose and interval keeps C~avg~ identical. Why is that not, by itself, evidence of anything?

Because it is arithmetic, not pharmacology. The same milligrams per unit time
give the same average concentration whatever the drug does. The evidence lives
entirely in the peak and trough: whether the trough still saturates the target,
and whether the peak has already been tolerated. A comparison table showing only
C~avg~ has shown you nothing.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. Your compound's exposure–response is steep over the studied range. What does that do to an exposure-matching argument?

It destroys it. Matching "closely" is only acceptable when the effect is
insensitive to the residual mismatch. On a steep curve, the between-subject
variability in exposure alone spans a meaningful difference in effect, and a
regimen change that shifts the distribution shifts outcomes. You need a trial, or
a different regimen that matches more tightly on the driving metric.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. A colleague proposes Q12W dosing at 800 mg on the grounds that C~avg~ matches exactly. What do you say?

That C~avg~ matching is guaranteed and therefore uninformative, and ask where the
peak and trough fall relative to the studied range. At Q12W the peak is likely
above any dose given in the programme and the trough below any observed, so the
exposure–response relationship has nothing to say about either. That is
extrapolation, and it needs data rather than simulation.
:::

## Going further

Lala M, Li TR, de Alwis DP, et al. *A six-weekly dosing schedule for
pembrolizumab in patients with cancer based on evaluation using modelling and
simulation.* Eur J Cancer 2020;131:68–75
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejca.2020.02.016)), with its corrigendum
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejca.2020.12.006)).

The underlying population PK model: Ahamadi M, Freshwater T, Prohn M, et al.
*Model-based characterization of the pharmacokinetics of pembrolizumab.* CPT
Pharmacometrics Syst Pharmacol 2016;6:49–57
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/psp4.12139), free full text) — built on
KEYNOTE-001, -002 and -006, and notable for finding that sex, performance
status, renal and hepatic measures, tumour type and burden all had **modest and
clinically insignificant** effects on exposure. That negative covariate result is
what licensed flat dosing.

For the class in general: Shang J, Huang L, Huang J, et al. *Population
pharmacokinetic models of anti-PD-1 mAbs in patients with multiple tumor types:
a systematic review.* Front Immunol 2022;13:871372
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.3389/fimmu.2022.871372), free full text).

`C-03` takes the companion case: nivolumab, where the exposure–response turned
out to be *flat* — which both licensed the regimen change and made the analysis
nearly uninformative about dose.
